transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-03-02
Start: 09:30 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Fernandez (Redwood SE), Noah Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Nimbus ML), Ethan Greene (Nimbus SRE), Dr. Laura Kim (Nimbus CTO)

Summary (auto): quick recap of pilot numbers; discussing session skew causing lower-than-expected prefix hit rates; tuning eviction and sticky-session configs; agreement to run 48h ramp with sticky sessions and share artifacts.

Topics: hit-rate breakdown, session-affinity, eviction thresholds, prefix coalescing, trace annotation, next run plan

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Okay, thanks everyone for joining. we'll call this the session skew and prefix reuse weekly check-in. quick round, who is on from Nimbus?
[00:07] Priya Rao: Hi, Priya here, ml eng. we ran the last set of traces over the weekend.
[00:10] Ethan Greene: Ethan, SRE. i got the kube side metrics, the p95 on the worker looked fine but tail did spike.
[00:15] Dr. Laura Kim: Laura here. i'm mostly listening but keen on the end-to-end latency impact.
[00:19] Maya Chen: Great. Luca, do you want to kick off with the numbers you pulled?
[00:23] Luca Fernandez: Sure. quick caveat, these are from the sample window 02/26-03/01, and some of the names in the traces were obfuscated so i had to map them. overall global KV hit-rate for prefix entries is at ~22% which is lower than expected; local prefix reuse (session keyed) is closer to 38% for returning sessions but we see big variance across user cohorts. so the headline is: prefix hit-rate underperforming vs model; causes look like session skew and noisy short-lived conversations.
[00:45] Priya Rao: yeah we saw that too — lots of single-turn interactions that never reuse prefix tokens. PTR by endpoint is uneven, and the chat flows with heavy tool calls kill prefix reuse.
[00:56] Noah Patel: just to add, the eviction policy was default LRU with a 30k entry cap — that means short bursts can push out longer-running session prefixes. if your traffic is bursty and not sticky, you lose reuse.
[01:10] Ethan Greene: that's what we suspected. we also were running without sticky_session=true in the first ramp to avoid affinity complexity. maybe that was a mistake.
[01:16] Maya Chen: Right. Two levers here: increase stickiness (session affinity) and adjust eviction/weighting to favor longer-lived prefixes. we also have prefix coalescing heuristics that can group similar prompts to improve hit rates — Luca, did you try that on a sample?
[01:30] Luca Fernandez: i did a small run — pre-fix coalescing (sorry, the auto-transcript sometimes hyphenates it) increased logical reuse by about +9 percentage points on a neighborhood of 15k traces, but it also added a small CPU decoding overhead on the shard. tradeoff is marginal latency increase of ~6-8ms median on generation start.
[01:51] Priya Rao: 6-8 ms is fine for us if net tokens saved are significant. can you quantify tokens saved?
[01:57] Luca Fernandez: in that sample we saw an average of ~72k tokens saved per 100k requests — roughly 0.72 tokens per request on median, with a long tail for sessions that reuse heavily.
[02:11] Dr. Laura Kim: how does this affect model variant choices? if we do more reuse, can we move to a cheaper quantized variant safely?
[02:19] Maya Chen: good question. reuse alone doesn't change model quality; it reduces token compute. earlier we recommended a hybrid approach: keep FP16 for critical paths and route high-reuse traffic to a quantized-friendly instance. also automatic fallback to full precision on quality regressions.
[02:33] Ethan Greene: can you remind us what routing rules look like? we have a mixture of webchat and internal API calls, we could tag them.
[02:40] Noah Patel: routing rule is basically a policy that looks at metadata: session_id present, user cohort tag, and historical hit_rate. high historical hit_rate routes to cheaper pool, low to default. we can make it conservative initially.
[02:50] Priya Rao: back to the hit-rate drop — you mentioned session skew. what exactly is skew in this context?
[02:55] Luca Fernandez: by skew i mean distribution shift across sessions — a small percentage of sessions generate most of the reuse (power law). If you don't pin sessions, prefixes get evicted while those long sessions expect the prefix to be present, so their hit-rate drops. it's visible in your trace where a session that spans 3 hours changes instance and loses KV entries.
[03:15] Ethan Greene: yep we saw cases where a user's chat window reconnects and goes to a different backend pod. we assumed autoscaling would handle that but the cache is per-pod in this deployment.
[03:25] Maya Chen: that suggests two mitigation paths: make the cache global/shared (but that's heavier and needs network overhead), or implement sticky session routing to keep sessions on the same pool. sticky session is lower operational lift.
[03:37] Priya Rao: what about TTL tuning? we currently have fairly short TTLs and aggressive eviction.
[03:43] Luca Fernandez: TTL helps if entries are long-lived, but TTL can't fix cross-pod eviction when affinity is lost. TTL tweak suggested: increase TTL for prefixes tagged as 'session-long' and add weight multiplier for prefixes from authenticated users. that will bias retention.
[03:57] Priya Rao: can we tag prefixes? how would that be done?
[04:00] Noah Patel: we can annotate the prefix key with metadata at insert time; Redwood's runtime supports a small metadata blob (like "session_length_hint": "long"). SEs can produce a script to mark traces where sessions exceed X minutes.
[04:12] Luca Fernandez: yes, and we ran a heuristic: if session > 10 minutes or >3 turns, mark as session-long. that bumped effective reuse for those keys by ~14 points in the sample.
[04:26] Maya Chen: good. quick check on instrumentation: do you have trace IDs for the cases where hit rate dropped from 70 to 15%?
[04:33] Ethan Greene: i uploaded a folder to the shared drive labeled "skew-traces-02-28". link in chat. most of the bad cases are between 01:00-03:00 UTC when your autoscaler did a scale-in.
[04:44] Priya Rao: also to call out — tool calls are a big noise source, and our extractor currently dumps tool output in prompt which prevents prefix matching.
[04:52] Luca Fernandez: we saw that. recommendation is to normalize tool responses out of the prefix key, or use a placeholder token so keys match across calls. that's a small payload change in the client.
[05:03] Priya Rao: that's doable. we'll need to push a change to the prompt builder.
[05:07] Maya Chen: action item: Redwood to share a sample prefix-normalization snippet and eviction JSON. we'll also share a tiny script to annotate the traces to isolate session-skew.
[05:16] Noah Patel: on the eviction policy, we proposed weighted-lru where weight = session_length_hint * (1 + reuse_count/10). that biases retention to high reuse prefixes. it doesn't require global cache.
[05:29] Ethan Greene: sounds reasonable. how does that affect memory? won't we keep more entries and blow the pod memory?
[05:34] Luca Fernandez: it's bounded — we keep the same cap but reorder eviction priority. you might see slightly higher median entry age which is fine. if you need hard caps we can add a soft-limit eviction to free lower-weight items more aggressively.
[05:49] Priya Rao: curious about metrics — what dashboards should we look at during the 48h ramp?
[05:54] Maya Chen: key ones: prefix KV hit-rate by cohort, per-session reuse distribution, per-pod eviction rate, tail latency (p95/p99) of first-token and stream-availability, and tokens saved per 100k requests. also have an alert on sudden drop in global hit-rate >10 points.
[06:11] Dr. Laura Kim: what about security/compliance — anything in cache metadata that might be PII?
[06:17] Maya Chen: by default we recommend not storing full user PII in cache keys; we advise hashing identifiers and using ephemeral session IDs. Redwood's KV cache supports opt-out for specific models — we can set redaction rules.
[06:29] Priya Rao: we have hashing implemented already, but will double check.
[06:32] Ethan Greene: ok can we go over the explicit run plan for the 48h test? what flags to flip?
[06:36] Luca Fernandez: plan: 1) enable sticky_session=true for webchat cohort only (Tag: webchat-beta), 2) enable prefix coalescing with conservative threshold, 3) set eviction to weighted-lru with session-long multiplier, 4) increase TTL to 45 minutes for session-long keys, 5) annotate traces with session_length_hint. Keep ramp at 20% traffic for first 6 hours then 50% next 18.
[07:02] Priya Rao: timeline ok. we'll change prompt-builder to normalize tool output and push client change tomorrow.
[07:08] Maya Chen: excellent. Luca, can you produce the small trace annotation script and the eviction JSON?
[07:12] Luca Fernandez: yes. i'll post both to the shared folder and ping. script will be a ~80 line python file that reads trace CSV and emits annotations. eviction JSON will include weights and ttl values.
[07:23] Priya Rao: when we flip sticky sessions, do we risk uneven CPU hot spots?
[07:28] Noah Patel: possible; that's why sticky is enabled only for webchat-beta and initial traffic is low. also we can set session affinity with soft balancing (stick for N minutes) so it's not permanent.
[07:38] Ethan Greene: what about a hybrid where we use a small globally-shared metadata store with lightweight pointers to local cache entries? is that supported?
[07:46] Luca Fernandez: we have an experiment called 'index pointers' where a lightweight global index references keys by id, enabling cross-pod lookup. it's more complex and has network overhead; we usually reserve it for enterprise deployments.
[07:59] Dr. Laura Kim: let's try stickiness first, and if hit-rate improves but tail latency spikes, we'll revisit index pointers.
[08:07] Maya Chen: agreed. quick Q from the team: are there any experiments we should avoid because of cost?
[08:12] Luca Fernandez: avoid global shared cache for the 48h ramp because networking cost and operational risk. prefix coalescing and weighted-lru are low risk. routing to quantized pools should be staged conservatively.
[08:23] Priya Rao: ok good. one more ask — can we get an estimated cost delta if hit-rate jumps from 22% to 45%? even a back-of-envelope helps our finance folks.
[08:31] Maya Chen: yes. Luca, can you run a quick unit econ calc?
[08:34] Luca Fernandez: rough calc: current token compute per 100k requests is X (we'll attach spreadsheet), if hit-rate doubles you can save roughly 18-25% in token compute spend depending on session distribution. i'll produce a short spreadsheet and include assumptions.
[08:48] Maya Chen: perfect. okay, let's do a rapid recap and next steps.
[08:52] Priya Rao: recap from Nimbus: prompt normalizer change pushed tomorrow; run 48h sticky_session ramp; upload metrics and traces.
[08:58] Maya Chen: recap from Redwood: share eviction JSON, prefix-normalization snippet, trace-annotation script, and the cost-back-of-envelope spreadsheet. we'll target sending these by 2027-03-05.
[09:08] Ethan Greene: one more thing — can we annotate the CRM with a note about potential enterprise interest if index pointers are needed?
[09:13] Maya Chen: noted — i'll add CRM note.
[09:15] Dr. Laura Kim: thanks all.
[09:17] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in the thread. bye.
